title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Food Safety Net
excerpt: Vietnam's dog meat trade operates with zero registered slaughterhouses, creating a public health crisis that 95% of Vietnamese want to end.
body_html:
In Vietnam, millions of people eat at restaurants every day with a reasonable expectation that the food on their plate has passed through some form of regulated inspection. That expectation does not apply to dog meat. Not a single dog meat slaughterhouse in Vietnam is formally registered or licensed. Every step of the supply chain — from capture to killing to consumption — operates entirely outside the country's food safety framework. This is not a gap in the system. It is the absence of one.

The consequences for public health are measurable and serious. Dogs moved through this trade are frequently transported across provincial borders without veterinary checks, creating ideal conditions for disease transmission. The World Health Organization has identified the dog meat trade as a vector for rabies spread, and studies have documented contamination with E. coli and Salmonella at processing and retail points. Unlike beef or pork supply chains — which, however imperfectly, involve licensing, inspection, and traceability — dog meat reaches the consumer with no documentation, no testing, and no accountability. When something goes wrong, there is no record of where the animal came from or who handled it.

Countries that have moved to ban or tightly regulate the dog meat trade offer a useful comparison. South Korea, which is actively legislating toward a full ban after decades of a regulated grey market, saw significant reductions in associated zoonotic disease risk as enforcement tightened. The Philippines enacted a ban in 1998 under its Animal Welfare Act, and subsequent public health data from regions where the trade was most active showed measurable declines in dog-related rabies transmission. The pattern is consistent: regulation and bans work, both for animals and for people.

What makes Vietnam's situation particularly significant is that the demand for change is not coming from outside the country. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade. That is not a fringe position or a foreign imposition — it is an overwhelming domestic consensus. Cities including Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have already issued formal recommendations to phase out the trade, citing both animal welfare and public health concerns. The regulatory infrastructure to act exists. What is needed now is the political will to apply it.

Lucky, a nine-year-old Vietnamese Tả dog and the face of the Stop Dog Eaters campaign, represents the millions of dogs whose lives depend on that political will becoming policy. But Lucky also represents something broader: the right of Vietnamese communities to live without the public health risks that an unregulated, uninspected food trade creates. Approximately 5 million dogs are killed in this trade every year. None of them pass through a single registered facility. Ending this trade is not about imposing external values — it is about enforcing the food safety and animal protection standards that Vietnam has already committed to on paper, backed by a population that is already on board.

🚨 Vietnam's dog meat trade: zero registered slaughterhouses. Zero inspections. Zero traceability.

• Every dog killed in this trade passes through a completely unregulated supply chain — no licensing, no veterinary checks, no food safety oversight
• The trade spreads rabies, E. coli, and Salmonella with no accountability system to trace outbreaks
• 95% of Vietnamese already support ending this trade — countries like the Philippines show that bans reduce zoonotic disease risk

This is a public health issue as much as an animal welfare one. It's time Vietnam's regulations caught up with its people.
